title: 3-Read Friday #94
author: Craig Barton
summary: Issue 94 of 3-Read Friday pairs a piece of assessment research with two pieces on the human and professional side of teaching. Barton opens with Katie Beynon and Dave Thomson's FFT Education Datalab research on how closely teachers' predicted GCSE grades matched pupils' actual results, previewing the counterintuitive spoiler that predictions track cohort averages well but are accurate for individual pupils less than half the time, with maths noticeably more predictable than English literature. He then highlights Claire Stoneman's 'Belonging, Part Two,' summarising her distinction between pastoral noticing (checking on lateness and wellbeing) and academic noticing (using mini whiteboards to see every child's thinking) as two complementary routes into the same goal of making children feel seen. The issue closes with Cati Wade's argument against the 'we already do that' excuse for skipping further professional learning, with Barton relaying her point that moving from initial adoption of a technique to genuine fidelity takes years, and that abandoning initiatives after a single term breeds 'initiative fatigue.' The throughline is teacher and school practice examined from three angles: measurement accuracy, relational culture, and professional learning discipline.
points: Barton's framing of the Beynon/Thomson research foregrounds the counterintuitive finding rather than a neutral description: predicted grades match cohort averages well but individual-pupil accuracy is below 50% in most subjects, with maths more predictable than English literature.

His summary of Stoneman's belonging piece distills a genuinely structural distinction -- pastoral noticing vs. academic noticing -- and captures her metaphor precisely: pastoral noticing 'anchors' belonging while academic noticing helps it 'set sail.'

Barton relays Wade's implementation-science point with specificity: moving from initial adoption to fidelity 'takes years,' directly undercutting the common school pattern of abandoning an initiative after a single term.

The issue's throughline links measurement (how well can we actually predict outcomes), relationships (how do we make students feel they belong), and professional discipline (how do we actually get better at what we already do) -- three angles on teaching practice rather than three unrelated topics.

Claire argues that children need to feel seen, valued, and noticed by their teachers. This isn’t about motivational posters or empty encouragement, but a genuine human connection through attention.

She distinguishes between pastoral noticing (checking on lateness, well-being) and academic noticing (using mini whiteboards to hear every child's thinking). Both forge belonging -- pastoral noticing anchors it, academic noticing helps it set sail.

Cati challenges the myth that if teachers “already do something,” there’s no point revisiting it. Implementation research shows moving from initial adoption to fidelity takes years, yet schools often abandon initiatives after a term, creating “initiative fatigue.
